Write a note to a friend about impressions from a trip abroad. Aim for about 400 words. Reply with the note only.
final_message:
My dear friend,

I have been home from my journey abroad for only a few days, but I wish to write to you at once, while the impressions are fresh, for I fear that in the press of daily duties they will fade before I have put them down.

The first thing that struck me was the order and the thoroughness with which the people go about their common work. I do not mean that everything is perfect; far from it. But I saw men and women in the shops, in the fields, and on the railways who seemed to put their whole conscience into whatever they had in hand, however small or humble it might be. A man who swept the street before his door swept it as if the eyes of the whole city were upon him. I confess that this lesson went home to me more than any cathedral or museum.

The second thing was the great respect shown to age and to authority. I do not say that every order given was a wise one, or that every person in authority was worthy of the place. Yet I noticed that the habit of obedience, and of courtesy toward those who have gone before, gave to the people a steadiness and a strength of character which I wish more of our young people could see. It is better, I am more than ever convinced, to learn to respect than to learn to criticise.

Then, too, there was the matter of economy. In many of the homes where I was received, there was no waste whatever. Every crust was used, every scrap of cloth was turned to some purpose. "Stretch a dollar," as we say at home, until it can be stretched no further--that seemed to be the rule of the household, and I could not but think how much we might gain if we followed it more closely.

I do not wish you to think that I came away with nothing but praise. There is poverty there, and there are difficulties which will take many years to overcome. But I found nothing to be discouraged about. The people are going forward, and they will keep going forward, so long as they do not let their hardships turn them from honest labor.

When you have an afternoon to spare, come and sit with me, and I shall tell you all the rest. I think that you will find it a convenient season to hear of it, and I shall be glad of your company.

Ever your friend,

T.
